title: What Our Backtest Says About the Senate Model
dek: Our model is still being tested, but the early results are positive. The main test uses saved 2024 model data, while the other test is a rough check meant to find problems before the full calibration update is finished.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: Our Senate model is still being tested, but the early results are encouraging.
When people look at a forecast, they usually ask one question first: did it pick the winner? That matters, but it is not enough. A good forecast also needs to give reasonable odds.

For example, if the model says a candidate has a 65 percent chance to win, then candidates with similar odds should win close to 65 percent of the time across many races. That is what we mean by calibration.
The calibration page currently has two different sections, and they are easy to mix up.

The first and more important section is the archived-input historical backtest. That means we use saved model inputs from an older election and check how the model would have done at the time. In simpler terms, it is the closest thing to asking: if this model existed before the election, how accurate would it have been?
That archived-input test is the main test readers should focus on.
Right now, the archived-input test only uses 11 races from the 2024 Senate cycle. That is a small sample, so it should not be treated as the final word. But it gives us a useful early check.

So far, the model has performed well in that test. In the 50 to 60 percent range, the model went 2 for 2. In the 60 to 70 percent range, it went 3 for 4. In the 70 to 80 percent range, it went 2 for 2. In the 80 to 90 percent range, it went 3 for 3.
That does not mean the model is perfect. A few races are not enough to prove that. But it does show that the model is placing races into reasonable probability ranges.

The second section is the current diagnostic. That word means a rough check for problems. It compares the current version of the model to older Senate results. This can help us find weak spots, but it is not the cleanest way to judge the model.

The current diagnostic has 35 races, which sounds better because the sample is larger. But the comparisons are less direct. Some states are being compared to races from 2016 or 2018. Some had very different candidates. Some had little polling. Some had independent candidates or special state-level factors.
That is why the current diagnostic should be used as a warning system, not as the main grade.

Even with those limits, the current diagnostic does not show a broken model. The 60 to 70 percent range had a 62.5 percent win rate, which is close to the expected 65 percent. The 90 to 100 percent range had a 95 percent win rate, exactly matching the expected 95 percent.

The weakest-looking part is the 80 to 90 percent range. In the current diagnostic, that range only had a 33.3 percent win rate. But that came from only three races, so it is too small to treat as proof of a major problem.

The archived-input margin misses also look normal. The largest misses were Pennsylvania at 5.2 points, Wisconsin at 4.2 points, Ohio at 3.6 points, Nebraska at 3.4 points, Nevada at 3.3 points, Florida at 2.8 points, Arizona at 2.6 points, and Montana at 2.1 points.

For Senate races, those misses are not alarming. Senate races are hard to forecast. Candidate strength, incumbency, polling quality, independent campaigns, and late movement all affect the final result. A model missing several races by two to five points is within a normal range.

The page also shows a Brier score. A Brier score is a way to measure how close the model's probabilities were to the final results. Lower is better. The current diagnostic shows a mean Brier score of 0.143. That is a useful number to track, but it should be read with the same caution as the rest of the current diagnostic.

The page also shows a mean margin miss of 12.5 points in the current diagnostic. That number looks high, but it comes from the rougher test, not the cleaner archived-input backtest. Some of those comparisons are not a fair one-to-one test of what the model would have forecast before a real election.

That is the main issue right now. The page has one section that is closer to a real backtest and another section that is more of a rough problem-checker. Both are useful, but they should not be read the same way.
By May 23, 2026, we plan to finish the calibration cleanup and make the page easier to understand. The update should separate the true backtest from the rough diagnostic more clearly.

After that update, readers should have a clearer answer to three questions. How did the model perform when tested against saved past-election inputs? Which numbers are only meant to catch possible problems? Which results should be used to judge the model?

The honest view is this: the model is not fully proven yet. More past cycles need to be added. Some probability ranges still have small samples. The current diagnostic includes some noisy comparisons.

But the evidence so far does not show a bad model. The cleaner archived-input test looks promising. The largest archived misses are reasonable. Several probability ranges are lining up well with the outcomes.

The model is still being improved, but the early signs are positive. For now, readers should use the archived-input backtest as the main score and use the current diagnostic as a tool for spotting possible weak points.
Once the May 23 calibration update is finished, the model should be easier to judge and easier for regular readers to understand.

title: How Dan Osborn has Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's Senate campaigns show a different path for Democrats in deep-red states. In places where the party label struggles, an independent with local credibility may perform better than a standard Democratic nominee.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: Dan Osborn has changed how you should think about deep-red Senate races.

Nebraska is not considered in any pathway to victory for Democrats in 2026 when it comes to the Senate. This is in large part because Republicans dominate the state. Democrats struggle in deep-red Nebraska due to negative brand recognition. AP reported that Nebraska Democrats in 2026 are looking for others who can "outperform the Democratic label."

Osborn is in a different form. He ran as an independent in 2024 and is running again in 2026. He leans on his background as a mechanic, Navy veteran, National Guardsman, and union leader. He campaigns on workers' rights, wages, corporate power, and taking money out of politics.

We saw what happened in 2024. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but the race was shockingly close historically in Nebraska. Fischer won by only about six points, while in 2024, the state voted for Donald Trump by over 20 points. What we learned was simple. Some voters who might reject national Democrats would still consider a candidate who sounds local, independent, and focused on economics.

Just last week, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in Nebraska. She campaigned simply on withdrawing and supporting Osborn. This reduces a split anti-Ricketts vote and avoids a three-way race, which all but guarantees Republicans hold on in the state.

Nebraska Democrats appeared to understand that when Nebraska's race focuses on the national aspect, Ricketts wins. When it goes local, Osborn stands to benefit. This is what Democrats need to study. Sometimes in a deep-red state, stepping aside is more strategic.

Of course, this does not work anywhere. You need someone with local credibility and a message voters believe. In a state where voters have histories of ticket splitting or independents, it might be the right move. However, national Democrats must stay disciplined. If these independents are turned into Republican versus not Republican, the brand is weakened.

Even if what the forecast model says holds, and Osborn loses, the current projected margin of only 3.9 points Republican shares a big message. Democrats must reinvent their strategies in the deep red, or become a figment of the past for those living in red states.
The takeaway should be clear. In deep-red states, Democrats need more flexibility. Sometimes the best Democratic move is to support a candidate who does not run as a Democrat.
